topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European digital public health context; competency frameworks may differ in other regions due to varying healthcare systems, regulatory environments, and digital maturity levels. Findings most applicable to European public health organisations.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies are prioritised across European public health systems to benchmark your organisation's current capability gaps against established frameworks.
Use the competency framework to structure targeted AI literacy training for public health staff, ensuring curricula align with recognised European standards rather than developing ad-hoc programmes.

Recognise that public health roles (epidemiologists, data analysts, policy makers) likely require different digital and AI competency levels — tailor your literacy programme by role rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to public health education context. Findings on faculty development approaches may transfer to other academic disciplines but sector-specific barriers and enablers in public health may not generalise broadly.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI literacy initiatives often stems from knowledge gaps rather than fundamental opposition—targeted professional development addressing specific concerns can shift educators from scepticism to readiness to teach AI competencies.

Institutional change in AI literacy requires investing in educator capability first; equipping faculty with confidence and practical skills in AI creates a ripple effect that improves student readiness and organisational culture around technology adoption.

Public health programs can use change management principles (addressing resistance, building coalitions among faculty champions, providing ongoing support) to embed AI literacy into curricula rather than treating it as an isolated add-on.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development requires adaptation.
takeaways: Design AI literacy programmes as part of a broader digital literacy framework rather than in isolation, ensuring foundational skills (data interpretation, computational thinking) precede applied AI use.

Middle school age represents a critical intervention point; consider whether your organisation's AI capability development includes scaffolded learning pathways that build progressively from fundamentals, as recommended for younger learners.
Integrate AI competencies across multiple subject areas or functional domains rather than siloing them in a single training module to improve retention and transfer of learning.

articles.title: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — discourse-based review likely drawing on international literature, but without specified geographic scope or empirical data, applicability depends on the specific healthcare contexts discussed.
takeaways: Understanding both AI pitfalls (e.g., bias, depersonalisation) and possibilities (e.g., efficiency gains) is essential before implementing AI in person-centred care settings; use this framing to structure stakeholder discussions with clinicians and patients about adoption concerns.

Person-centred care principles should drive AI implementation decisions rather than technology capability alone — audit current or planned AI tools against your organisation's values to identify misalignments early.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Likely focuses on higher education contexts; generalisability to corporate employee development in Australia would depend on whether recommendations address adult learning, workplace constraints, and industry-specific AI applications rather than academic curricula.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most critical for your workforce—technical skills, ethical understanding, and AI literacy may require different development pathways suited to employee roles and prior knowledge.

Higher education strategies often emphasise foundational knowledge and theory; extract principles applicable to workplace settings (e.g. experiential learning, cross-disciplinary collaboration) and adapt them to your organisational context and learning timeline.

articles.title: AI literacy in undergraduate medical education: a competency-based interpretive framework for curriculum and assessment - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy in undergraduate medical education: a competency-based interpretive framework for curriculum and assessment  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on medical education curriculum design, which may not directly transfer to corporate AI literacy programs. Findings are specific to undergraduate medical training contexts and may not generalise to other professional sectors or organisational settings.
takeaways: Use a competency-based framework to structure AI literacy programs — define specific, measurable capabilities employees should develop rather than generic 'AI awareness' modules.

Integrate assessment methods aligned with learning objectives; the medical education model suggests combining knowledge checks, practical application scenarios, and capability demonstrations rather than single-format training evaluation.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from title and snippet alone — full geographic scope and sample characteristics cannot be determined. Likely limited to specific sectors or organisational contexts studied.
takeaways: AI adoption can have paradoxical effects on employee creativity — understanding both positive and negative mechanisms is essential before implementation to design interventions that maximise creative output.
Organisations should assess whether their current AI tools are augmenting creative thinking or constraining it through over-automation or deskilling, and adjust deployment strategies accordingly.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing roles and medical AI contexts; generalisability to other healthcare professions or sectors unclear without more detail on sample composition and geographic location.
takeaways: Preserve and expand work autonomy as you implement AI systems in clinical settings — autonomy appears to be the key mechanism linking AI readiness to staff wellbeing, not AI readiness alone.
When assessing nurse readiness for medical AI adoption, measure psychological wellbeing outcomes alongside technical competence, and monitor whether autonomy is being eroded by AI implementation.
Design AI workflows that augment rather than constrain clinical decision-making; loss of autonomy may offset the benefits of improved AI readiness on employee wellbeing.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the snippet provided; geographic scope, sample size, and sector details are not evident. Further review of the full article methods section would be needed to determine applicability.
takeaways: Address role ambiguity explicitly when introducing generative AI tools — clarify which tasks AI should handle, which remain human-owned, and how collaboration will work in practice, as unclear roles undermine adoption.

Build employee self-efficacy through structured training and early wins with AI tools before scaling adoption; employees with stronger belief in their ability to work effectively with AI are more likely to collaborate productively rather than resist or misuse the technology.

Design change management around both reducing uncertainty (role clarity) and building confidence (self-efficacy), as these are independent psychological pathways that each influence how employees embrace or reject AI collaboration.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — likely limited to specific organizational contexts or regions where paternalistic leadership is prevalent; generalizability to Western, non-paternalistic organizations uncertain.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by involving employees in customizing or 'crafting' AI features to their workflows — this sense of ownership increases collaboration willingness even under directive leadership styles.
Paternalistic leaders can leverage AI adoption by framing AI implementation as a supportive intervention tailored to team needs, rather than a top-down mandate, to strengthen employee buy-in.

Design AI onboarding programs that allow hands-on adaptation and personalization of tools; this agency appears to mediate the relationship between leadership style and actual employee-AI collaboration.

articles.title: When humans and agents form a collective: a framework for collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When humans and agents form a collective: a framework for collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents a conceptual framework rather than empirical validation. Applicability depends on how well the framework generalizes across different organizational contexts, team sizes, and AI agent types.
takeaways: Use this framework to assess whether your human-AI teams are optimized for collective intelligence — check that role clarity, communication protocols, and decision-making structures are explicitly designed for human-agent collaboration rather than treating AI as a tool.

Consider implementing structured feedback loops and trust-building mechanisms between team members and AI agents to support the 'persistent' nature of these teams, since sustained collaboration requires evolving relationships.

Map your current human-AI team composition against the framework's dimensions to identify gaps — e.g., whether your team has mechanisms for shared mental models, mutual accountability, or adaptive task allocation between humans and agents.

articles.title: The impact of generative AI use on employees’ psychological distress: a moderated mediation model - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of generative AI use on employees’ psychological distress: a moderated mediation model  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not disclosed in the snippet. The moderated mediation model is theoretically sound but findings may be limited by sector, organisational context, and geographic scope — details needed to assess applicability to Australian workplaces.
takeaways: Psychological distress from AI adoption is not uniform across employees — identify and support those at highest risk by understanding which individual or contextual factors moderate the AI-distress relationship in your organisation.

The pathway from AI use to distress is mediated (indirect), meaning distress arises through intervening mechanisms such as role clarity, skill gaps, or autonomy loss — target interventions at these mediators rather than AI use itself.

Conduct a parallel assessment in your team to map how generative AI adoption is affecting psychological wellbeing, then design targeted upskilling, change communication, and psychological safety initiatives based on your specific risk profile.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner insights are based on consulting experience but lack detail on specific sample size, sectors, or geographies. Findings likely generalizable to large organizations with resources for structured change management, but applicability to smaller Australian firms or specific sectors unclear.
takeaways: Distinguish between 'adoption' (getting people to use AI) and 'adaptation' (helping them develop new behaviours and mindsets for effective AI use) — treating these as separate change phases improves success rates.
Design behaviour change interventions that target the human side (culture, skills, confidence, role redesign) in parallel with technology rollout, not after it.

Map which specific work behaviours and mental models need to shift for your team (e.g. from command-and-control to collaborative human-AI workflows), then build targeted learning and reinforcement into your change plan.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a perspective piece from Stanford GSB without specified empirical scope. Findings and recommendations may not generalise beyond US-based business contexts.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation will experience the most significant AI-driven changes, then design targeted upskilling programs before disruption occurs rather than reacting to it.
Create communication strategies that address employee anxiety about AI adoption by emphasising role transformation rather than replacement, helping teams envision how they'll work alongside AI tools.
Establish feedback loops with employees as AI tools are implemented to surface real-world usability issues and capability gaps early, allowing you to adjust change management approaches.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Broad applicability across sectors, though based on McKinsey's client base which skews toward large enterprises. Findings may not fully represent small-to-medium organisations or non-profit contexts.
takeaways: Map your AI transformation across three distinct horizons — immediate wins, scaling capability, and transformational impact — to avoid treating adoption as the end goal and ensure sustained behaviour change and value realisation.

Design change management interventions that evolve with each horizon: early adoption requires building confidence and quick wins; scaling needs standardised processes and role clarity; transformation demands culture shift and long-term capability embedding.

Identify and address the specific barriers at each horizon — from skills gaps in horizon one to organisational silos in horizon two to misaligned incentives in horizon three — rather than applying one-size-fits-all change strategies.

articles.title: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Are all digital hoarding behavior alike? Uncovering the pathways to digital hoarding behavior in the workplace  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to the full article, generalisability cannot be fully assessed. The specific geographic scope, sample size, and sector coverage are unclear from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Digital hoarding (excessive file retention, duplicate storage, disorganised digital assets) may stem from multiple distinct psychological pathways — understanding which pathway drives an individual's behaviour is essential before designing targeted intervention strategies.

Organisations seeking to reduce digital hoarding should diagnose the root causes first (e.g., fear of data loss, perfectionism, lack of organisation skills, or low digital literacy) to tailor change initiatives effectively rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — limited geographic scope information provided. The study applies theoretical frameworks (JD-R model, cognitive appraisal theory) that are well-established in occupational psychology, but the specific sample characteristics and cultural context are not evident from the title and snippet.
takeaways: AI awareness can trigger two distinct pathways in how employees reshape their work: one through stress appraisal (threat vs. challenge perception) and one through resource and demand balancing — understanding which pathway dominates in your team helps tailor upskilling interventions.

Employees who appraise AI as a challenge rather than a threat are more likely to proactively craft their roles (e.g., seek new skills, reframe tasks) — framing AI adoption conversations around opportunity rather than displacement may shift employee agency and engagement.

Job crafting (employees redesigning their own work scope and meaning) appears to be a measurable outcome of how employees cognitively process AI in their workplace — tracking job crafting behaviours could serve as an early indicator of whether your AI change strategy is landing as intended.

articles.title: The impact of generative AI use on employees’ psychological distress: a moderated mediation model - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of generative AI use on employees’ psychological distress: a moderated mediation model  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability is unclear without access to full text; likely limited by unspecified sample composition, geography, and sector. The moderated mediation model may not transfer to organisations with different AI adoption contexts or workforce demographics.
takeaways: Psychological distress from generative AI use isn't direct — it operates through intermediate mechanisms (likely job uncertainty, skill anxiety, or role ambiguity) that can be targeted with specific interventions.

Moderation effects suggest distress outcomes depend on contextual factors (e.g. organisational support, training quality, or job security measures) — tailor change management strategies to your workplace context rather than assuming universal outcomes.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — news report summarising research findings without details on sample size, methodology, or geographic scope. Readers should consult the original peer-reviewed study for rigorous assessment of generalisability.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies show detectable neurological differences in people with psychopathic traits, making it tempting to think we can 'scan for psychopathy' — but the real story is messier: individual variation is huge, and brain differences don't neatly map onto behaviour.

The 'shocking difference' framing is classic science communication — the actual finding is likely more nuanced (e.g. reduced activity in specific regions, altered connectivity patterns) than headlines suggest, reminding us to dig into methodology before drawing conclusions.

This research highlights how neuroscience can reveal biological correlates of personality and behaviour, but biology is never destiny — environmental factors, socialisation, and context all shape outcomes in ways brain scans alone cannot capture.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — twin studies provide insights into genetic contributions but findings depend heavily on the specific population studied (likely Western, developed country). Generalisability to non-Western political contexts or different cultural frameworks is unclear.
takeaways: Authoritarian political beliefs have a measurable genetic component, meaning political orientation isn't purely learned or chosen — it's partly rooted in inherited traits.
This finding is counterintuitive because we typically think of political beliefs as entirely shaped by family upbringing, media, and personal experience, yet biology plays a surprising role.

The nature-versus-nurture debate in politics is far more nuanced than 'nature vs. nurture' — both genetic predisposition and environment interact, which challenges simplistic assumptions about why people hold the political views they do.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited without access to full methodology — unable to determine sample size, geographic scope, or whether findings generalise beyond the specific experimental conditions tested.
takeaways: People don't all remember surprising moments the same way — your personality shapes what sticks in your memory when something unexpected happens.
This challenges the common assumption that shocking or surprising events are equally memorable for everyone, suggesting individual traits play a bigger role than we typically assume.

It's a fun window into why two people can witness the exact same surprising event and walk away with completely different recollections — personality is quietly directing what our brains decide to keep.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unknown without full article — appears to be a news report on research findings rather than primary research documentation.
takeaways: What we write about trivial preferences like wine reveals measurable personality traits — suggesting our everyday language choices are more psychologically diagnostic than we might assume.
AI text analysis can uncover hidden patterns in how people describe subjective experiences, opening new windows into personality research beyond traditional questionnaires.
A fun reminder that personality psychology isn't confined to formal assessments — it's lurking in your book reviews, restaurant recommendations, and wine notes.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Likely high — Cambridge research on global musical preferences suggests cross-cultural patterns, though specific sample composition and size are not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: People with similar personality types gravitate toward the same genres worldwide, suggesting personality-music links transcend cultural boundaries.
Your Spotify playlist might reveal more about your personality than you think — and it probably matches millions of strangers on the other side of the world.
Music taste acts as a universal personality fingerprint, which is both surprising (given how culturally varied music is) and oddly reassuring about human psychological commonality.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews MBTI research broadly, but findings reflect limitations of MBTI itself as a predictive tool, which has been widely criticized in industrial-organizational psychology for weak psychometric properties.
takeaways: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, beloved by millions for self-discovery, turns out to be surprisingly poor at actually predicting who will be a good leader — a humbling reminder that popular personality frameworks aren't the same as rigorous science.

Despite MBTI's cultural ubiquity in corporate training and team-building, the evidence suggests your four-letter type doesn't reliably tell you whether someone will inspire, manage conflict, or make sound decisions.
This highlights a fun paradox: we love categorizing ourselves into neat personality boxes, but leadership effectiveness is messier and more context-dependent than any single typology can capture.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methods — limited by lack of information on sample size, geographic scope, and sectors studied. The causal mechanisms identified may not apply uniformly across different organisational contexts or countries with different AI adoption trajectories.
takeaways: AI adoption without concurrent investment in psychological safety and ethical leadership can increase employee depression risk — prioritise safety and transparent ethical frameworks before or alongside AI implementation.

Psychological safety acts as a protective factor in AI transitions; create explicit permission for employees to voice concerns about AI impact on their role, capabilities, and wellbeing without fear of repercussion.

Ethical leadership during AI adoption is critical — leaders must visibly model and communicate the ethical principles guiding AI use, helping employees understand the 'why' and 'how' to reduce anxiety and disengagement.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — while BCG's insights draw from consulting work with global clients, the snippet provides limited detail on sample size, sectors covered, or geographic distribution of organizations studied.
takeaways: Frame psychological safety as an equity lever: organizations can use it intentionally to reduce hierarchical barriers and create more equitable opportunities for underrepresented or quieter employees to contribute and be heard.

Measure the 'playing field effect' in your team: assess whether psychological safety correlates with more balanced participation across demographic groups, seniority levels, and personality types in meetings and decisions.

Address structural barriers alongside cultural ones: psychological safety alone won't level the field if processes, norms, or decision-making still favour dominant voices—audit your team's interaction patterns explicitly.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: High — global survey captures workforce sentiment across multiple countries and sectors, though specific methodological details (sample size, response rate, sector weighting) are not visible from the snippet provided. Findings likely reflect perspectives from developed economies where PwC operates.
takeaways: Use workforce sentiment data to identify psychological safety gaps: survey findings on employee fears and hopes can reveal specific trust deficits in your organisation that require targeted interventions (e.g., transparency about AI adoption, job security communication).

Benchmark your organisation's psychological safety climate against global trends: compare how your employees express fears and hopes to the 2026 global data to identify whether your culture lags peer organisations in creating safe speaking-up environments.

Address fear narratives proactively in change communication: if the survey reveals widespread workforce anxiety about technology or leadership, use these insights to design reassurance campaigns and safety-building initiatives before fear undermines trust.

articles.title: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty - MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.snippet: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty  MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents conceptual framework and principles applicable across contexts, but lacks empirical validation or specific organisational case studies to demonstrate impact in different sectors or geographies.
takeaways: Create explicit norms where people are expected to voice dissenting views and challenge assumptions without fear of retaliation—frame this as essential to innovation, not insubordination.
Model intellectual honesty from leadership by openly acknowledging uncertainty, admitting mistakes, and engaging genuinely with contrary evidence rather than defending positions defensively.

Establish structured feedback mechanisms (e.g., pre-mortems, devil's advocate roles, anonymous input channels) that make it psychologically safe to surface bad news, flawed reasoning, or unpopular ideas early in innovation cycles.

articles.title: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess without full article access — snippet provides only title and journal name. Generalisability depends on study design, sample composition, and geographic scope, which are not evident from the limited information provided.
takeaways: Psychological safety may be undermined if AI implementation reduces perceived control or increases uncertainty about job security — proactive communication about AI's role and worker agency is critical.
Monitor team affective well-being (mood, stress, confidence) during AI transitions as a leading indicator of psychological safety; address emotional concerns alongside technical capability-building.

Create forums where employees can safely voice concerns about AI's impact on their work without fear of appearing resistant or incompetent — this directly supports both psychological safety and well-being.

articles.title: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Empowering workforces in AI-driven environments: co-skilling, organizational support, and mitigating job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — draws on existing literature but specific geographic scope and sector applicability unclear from title alone. Findings likely generalizable across developed economies with significant AI adoption, but regional labour market differences may limit applicability.
takeaways: Implement structured co-skilling programmes that pair AI upskilling with role-specific training to reduce psychological threat and build employee confidence in AI-driven transitions.

Create visible organizational support mechanisms (mentoring, transparent career pathways, reskilling investment) that directly address job insecurity concerns and signal management commitment to employee retention.

Use psychological safety initiatives alongside technical training — employees who feel psychologically safe are more likely to engage with upskilling and view AI as a collaborative tool rather than a threat.
